meta.tagline: Fashion, design, football and the best aperitivo on earth — in that order

overview.title: Welcome to Milano
overview.intro: Milan doesn't try to charm you. It doesn't need to. This is a working city — Italy's financial and fashion capital, full of people with somewhere to be, performing for no one. But just beneath that cool surface, something else entirely is going on: Leonardo da Vinci's greatest masterpiece on a convent wall, a Gothic cathedral six centuries in the making, a colony of flamingos living in a private garden two blocks from the city centre, and an aperitivo culture so generous it amounts to a free dinner with every drink. Milan takes a moment to open up. Give it that moment.

local_word.definition: Not just a drink before dinner — a social institution. Every evening from 6 to 9 PM, Milano's bars transform: order one drink and a spread of food appears. In some places it's a full buffet. In others, just a few bites. Either way, it's the city's great democratic ritual — the moment when finance directors and art students sit at the same bar and the evening properly begins.

rules.title: Book everything that matters in advance
rules.description: Leonardo's Last Supper (Santa Maria delle Grazie) is one of the most regulated visits in the world — only 30 people allowed in at a time, 15 minutes maximum. Tickets sell out weeks, sometimes months ahead. Il Duomo rooftop, the Pinacoteca di Brera, Cenacolo Vinciano — book all of these before you arrive. Walking up on the day guarantees disappointment.

rules.title: Aperitivo is not a snack — it is dinner
rules.description: Milanese aperitivo begins at 18:00 and runs until around 21:00. Order a Spritz, Negroni or Campari Soda and a spread of food arrives — sometimes a full buffet, always substantial. This is how the city eats on weekday evenings. Don't eat before. Don't rush it. Sit, drink, graze, and watch Milano decompress after work.

rules.title: Sunday shuts down — plan around it
rules.description: More than most Italian cities, Milano observes Sunday. Shops close, many restaurants shut, the fashion district goes quiet. The upside: museums are less crowded, parks fill with locals, and the city shows a slower, more residential face. Plan your museum visits and park days for Sunday and your shopping for any other day.

quick_facts.label: Airport
quick_facts.sub: Linate · 30 min · city center · Malpensa · 50 min · Malpensa Express

quick_facts.label: Transport
quick_facts.sub: ATM day pass covers all lines

quick_facts.label: Aperitivo
quick_facts.sub: One drink, unlimited food. The city's best meal.

quick_facts.label: Dress code
quick_facts.sub: Not a rule — a culture. Dress well and the city opens up.

tip.label: The real Milano
tip.text: Milan rewards slowness disguised as efficiency. The Milanese move fast but live well. Don't rush from landmark to landmark — find a neighbourhood, find a bar, order a Campari, and let the city reveal itself at its own pace. The best Milan is the one you stumble into.

transport.title: Getting Around
transport.intro: Milano has one of Italy's best public transport networks. The metro is clean, fast and logical. Between metro, trams and buses, almost everything is reachable without a taxi.

items.title: Linate Airport (LIN) → City Center
items.description: Linate is the closest airport — just 7 km from the city center. The metro Line 4 (M4, blue line) opened in 2023 and connects Linate directly to the center in about 30 minutes. Bus 73 is the budget alternative but slower. Taxi is expensive. If you're flying into Linate, the M4 is the obvious choice.

items.title: Malpensa Airport (MXP) → City Center
items.description: Malpensa is 50 km northwest of the city — further but handles more international flights. The Malpensa Express train runs directly to Milano Centrale (50 min) or Cadorna (40 min) every 30 minutes. It's the fastest and most reliable option. Shared shuttles exist but add significant time. Taxis from Malpensa are very expensive.

items.title: Metro — fast and logical
items.description: Milano's metro has four lines (M1 red, M2 green, M3 yellow, M4 blue) covering all major areas. It's fast, clean and runs until midnight on weekdays, later on weekends. Tap your contactless card or buy a single journey or day pass at any station. The day pass is excellent value if you're making more than three journeys. Validate before boarding.

items.title: Trams — the authentic way
items.description: Milano's historic orange trams are one of the city's most charming features — some have been running since the 1920s. They're slower than the metro but cover areas the underground doesn't reach and offer a moving view of the city. Line 1 from Piazza Castello to Piazza XXIV Maggio is one of the great urban tram rides in Europe. Same ticket as the metro.

items.title: BikeMi — city bikes
items.description: Milano's public bike share system with hundreds of docking stations throughout the city. Excellent for flat central areas, canal-side rides along the Navigli, and reaching the Parco Sempione from the center. Register online or via the app. Electric bikes also available at select stations.

callout.label: ATM day pass
callout.text: If you're spending a full day in the city, the ATM day pass covers unlimited journeys on metro, trams and buses. Buy it at any metro station or tabacchi. Far better value than individual tickets if you're moving around — and you will be.

stay.title: Where to Stay
stay.intro: Milano's neighbourhoods are dramatically different in character. The right choice depends entirely on what kind of city you want to wake up in.

local_word.definition: The canal district in southwest Milano — once Leonardo da Vinci's engineering project, now the city's most bohemian neighbourhood. The two main canals, Naviglio Grande and Naviglio Pavese, are lined with bars, restaurants, antique shops and ateliers. On the last Sunday of the month, the Mercatone dell'Antiquariato fills the entire canal bank with one of Italy's great flea markets.

items.name: Brera
items.description: Milano's most picturesque neighbourhood — cobblestone streets, art galleries, independent boutiques, the magnificent Pinacoteca di Brera. Central, walkable and effortlessly elegant. The aperitivo bars here are some of the best in the city. More expensive than other areas but genuinely one of the finest urban neighbourhoods in Italy.

items.name: Navigli
items.description: The canal district. Bohemian, creative and alive at all hours. The Naviglio Grande and Naviglio Pavese canals are lined with bars, restaurants and studios. The aperitivo scene here is legendary — some of the most generous spreads in the city. Slightly further from Il Duomo but the metro brings you there in minutes. The last-Sunday flea market is unmissable.

items.name: Isola
items.description: Once a working-class island cut off by railway lines, Isola is now Milano's most interesting neighbourhood — independent restaurants, design studios, street art and the spectacular Bosco Verticale (Vertical Forest) towers. Genuinely local, genuinely creative, not yet overrun. The area around Piazza Garibaldi and Corso Como is one of the best in the city.

items.name: Porta Romana & Tortona
items.description: The city's design and fashion heartland — particularly electric during Salone del Mobile in April. Former industrial buildings now house the city's most important galleries, showrooms and concept stores. The Fondazione Prada is here. Quieter outside design week but deeply interesting year-round.

items.name: Città Studi
items.description: The university district east of the center. Young, affordable and genuinely local — good trattorias, neighbourhood bars, the wonderful Orto Botanico. Further from the tourist sights but well connected by metro and tram. The area around Piazza Leonardo da Vinci has a calm, studious energy that's very different from the fashion-district intensity.

best_time.title: Best Time to Visit
best_time.intro: Milano is a city of seasons — each one transforms its character completely. The fashion and design calendar also shapes the city's rhythm in ways worth knowing.

items.label: Spring
items.name: Design Week
items.subtitle: Spring · Design Week & Perfect Weather
items.description: April brings Salone del Mobile — the world's most important design fair — and Milano transforms entirely. The whole city becomes a design exhibition, with events, installations and parties spilling out of every corner. Outside design week, spring offers ideal weather, cherry blossoms in the Parco Sempione and a city in full energy. The most exciting time to be here.

callout.label: Don't miss
callout.text: Salone del Mobile (April): the fair itself is enormous but the real action is the Fuorisalone — hundreds of events across the city, most of them free. The Brera Design District and Tortona are the epicenters.

items.label: Summer
items.name: Hot & Local
items.subtitle: Summer · Hot, Quiet, Surprisingly Local
items.description: August is when Milanese leave for the coast or mountains and the city empties. Restaurants close, streets quiet down, and a strange calm descends on one of Europe's most frenetic cities. July is hot and humid but perfectly functional — fewer tourists, shorter queues, lower prices. The aperitivo scene continues regardless. Not the conventional peak season but has its own particular charm.

callout.label: August warning
callout.text: Many restaurants and shops close for 2–3 weeks in mid-August (Ferragosto). Always check ahead. The upside: museums are emptier than at any other time of year.

items.label: Autumn
items.name: Fashion Week
items.subtitle: Autumn · Fashion Week & Golden Light
items.description: September brings Milano Fashion Week — the city's other great transformation. The streets fill with editors, buyers and photographers; restaurants become impossible without reservations; the energy is electric. Outside fashion week, September and October offer golden light, harvest produce in the markets, and a city settling into its most liveable season.

callout.label: Don't miss
callout.text: Milano Fashion Week (September): you don't need an invitation to experience it. The street outside shows is a spectacle in itself. Position yourself near the shows in Brera and watch the world's best-dressed people arrive.

items.label: Winter
items.name: Misty & Magical
items.subtitle: Winter · Fog, Risotto & La Scala
items.description: Milano in winter is fog, candlelit trattorias, risotto milanese and the extraordinary La Scala opera season. The city is at its most intimate — locals only, tourists few, the fashion district quiet. Christmas markets in Piazza Duomo and along the Navigli. January is the quietest and most authentic month. February brings carnival and the first design-week energy begins building.

callout.label: Local secret
callout.text: La Scala's season runs October to July, with the most prestigious premieres in December. Last-minute tickets sometimes appear on the official website. Even standing-room is an extraordinary experience.

monthly_highlights.text: Salone del Mobile + Design Week: the world's design capital for one week; open-air installations everywhere, hotels fill early.
Fashion Week: the streets become a runway; the Quadrilatero for celebrity spotting, people-watching heaven for everyone else.
Sant'Ambrogio + Oh Bej! Oh Bej!: the patron saint's day, the traditional market and La Scala's opening night — Milan's most Milanese day.
Summer evenings: Navigli and Isola stay out late; in mid-August the city belongs to the locals and many shops go on holiday.

eat.title: What to Eat
eat.intro: Milano's food is nothing like the rest of Italy — and Milanese are proud of that. Richer, slower-cooked, more influenced by the north. This is the city that invented risotto, cotoletta and panettone.

local_word.definition: The city's signature dish — Carnaroli rice, bone marrow, white wine, saffron and an almost violent amount of Parmigiano. The saffron turns it a deep gold. It's not a side dish. Ordering it correctly means asking for it as a primo (first course) and waiting the full 18 minutes it takes to make properly. Any risotto that arrives in under 10 minutes was not made for you.

items.name: Risotto alla Milanese — the city's signature
items.description: Saffron-gold, bone-marrow-rich, finished with a generous hand of Parmigiano. The real thing takes 18 minutes from order to plate and arrives slightly liquid — all'onda, they say, like a wave. If it's stiff, it's been sitting. Osteria dell'Acquabella and Trattoria del Nuovo Macello are benchmarks. Order it as a primo, not a side.

items.name: Cotoletta alla Milanese — not a schnitzel
items.description: Bone-in veal cutlet, breaded and fried in clarified butter until deeply golden. Thicker than Wiener Schnitzel, richer, and always served with the bone attached. The debate about whether the Viennese stole the recipe from Milano has been running for 200 years. Order it at a traditional trattoria, not a tourist restaurant. It should be crisp, substantial and arrive alone.
items.tag: Bone-in · butter-fried · not a side dish

items.name: Cassoeula — winter in a bowl
items.description: The definitive winter dish: pork (ribs, sausage, trotters) slow-cooked with Savoy cabbage until everything collapses into something profound and deeply comforting. Only on menus from October to February — if you see it any other time, it's not real. Order it in a trattoria in the Navigli or Porta Romana. It's heavy, honest and deeply Milanese.

items.name: Colazione Milanese — the breakfast ritual
items.description: Stand at the bar (never sit — it costs more and misses the point). Order a cappuccino and a cornetto (Italian croissant, filled with cream, jam or pistachio). The whole thing takes four minutes and costs very little. Repeat at any bar in the city. This is how 9 million journeys begin every morning in Lombardy.
items.tag: Stand at the bar · cappuccino + cornetto · never before 7 AM

items.name: Aperitivo — the Milanese invention
items.description: The city that gave the world Campari (invented here in 1860) takes its aperitivo seriously. The classic order: Campari Soda, Negroni or Aperol Spritz. At most bars, one drink unlocks the food spread. In Navigli and Brera, the spreads can be extraordinary — pasta, rice dishes, bruschetta, charcuterie. This is dinner, priced as a drink.

items.name: Panettone — the original
items.description: Yes, panettone is from Milano. The original is nothing like the supermarket versions exported around the world — tall, domed, made with a natural yeast starter that takes days to develop. Pasticceria Marchesi (founded 1824) and Pasticceria Cova are the historic benchmarks. Even outside Christmas, good Milanese bakeries carry it year-round.
items.tag: Marchesi or Cova · the original is nothing like the export version

callout.label: Mercato Comunale di Porta Romana
callout.text: Milano has exceptional food markets. The Mercato Comunale di Porta Romana is one of the best — a covered market where local producers sell cheese, charcuterie, fresh pasta, vegetables and wine. Go on Saturday morning, arrive hungry, and buy your lunch there. Far better than any restaurant at a fraction of the cost.

hidden_gems.title: Hidden Corners
hidden_gems.intro: Milano rewards those who look beyond Il Duomo and the Galleria. The city's most extraordinary things are behind unmarked doors, inside converted factories and at the end of quiet courtyards.

items.rarity: Leonardo's other masterpiece — almost no queue
items.name: The Last Supper (Cenacolo Vinciano) — Santa Maria delle Grazie
items.description: Everyone knows it exists. Almost no one prepares for how extraordinary it is in person. Painted directly onto the refectory wall between 1495 and 1498, it is 8.8 metres wide and nearly 5 metres tall. You stand in front of it for exactly 15 minutes with 29 other people in a climate-controlled room. The experience is unlike anything else in Italy. Book weeks ahead — but book.

items.rarity: Secret garden inside a Renaissance courtyard
items.name: Università degli Studi — Cortile della Facoltà di Giurisprudenza
items.description: The central courtyard of Milano's historic university, built on the site of a 15th-century hospital designed by Filarete. Walk through the unmarked entrance on Via Festa del Perdono and find a perfectly preserved Renaissance courtyard where students have studied for 600 years. Almost entirely unknown to tourists. Free, open during university hours.

items.rarity: The most beautiful bookshop in Italy
items.name: Libreria Bocca — Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II
items.description: Inside the Galleria, hidden from the luxury shops and tourist crowds, is Italy's oldest bookshop — open since 1775. The interior is magnificent: dark wood, glass cases, art books stacked floor to ceiling. Specialises in art, architecture and design. The staff have been recommending books since before most countries existed. Go in, even if you don't buy anything.

items.rarity: Vertical forest — a building like no other
items.name: Bosco Verticale — Isola
items.description: Two residential towers in the Isola neighbourhood covered in 900 trees, 5,000 shrubs and 11,000 plants — a forest suspended above the city. Designed by Stefano Boeri and completed in 2014, they have become one of the most photographed buildings in the world. You can't go inside but they are extraordinary from street level. The surrounding neighbourhood of Isola is worth half a day in itself.

items.rarity: Fondazione Prada — art in a distillery
items.name: Fondazione Prada
items.description: Miuccia Prada's extraordinary foundation occupies a former gin distillery in the Porta Romana area — a complex of old and new buildings designed by Rem Koolhaas's OMA. The permanent collection includes some of the most significant contemporary art in Italy. The gold-leafed Haunted House building alone is worth the visit. The Bar Luce, designed by Wes Anderson to look like a 1950s Milanese café, is exceptional.

items.rarity: The oldest canal in Europe — for a sunset walk
items.name: Naviglio Grande at golden hour
items.description: Leonardo da Vinci worked on the canal system here in the late 15th century. The Naviglio Grande — stretching 50 km to the Ticino river — was once how marble arrived in Milano to build Il Duomo. Today it's lined with bars, restaurants and studios. At golden hour, the light on the water and the reflections of the old buildings create one of the most beautiful urban scenes in northern Italy. Walk from the Darsena west toward Corsico.

callout.label: Last Sunday of the month
callout.text: On the last Sunday of every month, the Mercatone dell'Antiquariato fills the entire length of Naviglio Grande — one of Italy's greatest flea markets. Antique dealers, vintage clothing, art prints, furniture, ceramics. Arrive early. Bring cash. It runs from early morning until evening and is one of the most genuinely Milanese experiences available.

items.label: Book The Last Supper before anything else
items.sub: Santa Maria delle Grazie. 15 minutes, 30 people, weeks to book. Do it now.

items.label: Have aperitivo in Navigli or Brera
items.sub: One drink, full food spread. 18:00–21:00. This is dinner.

items.label: Order risotto alla Milanese as a primo
items.sub: 18 minutes to make. Saffron gold. Slightly liquid. If it arrives fast, it's wrong.

items.label: Walk through Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II
items.sub: One of the most beautiful covered arcades in the world. Spin on the bull for luck.

items.label: Go inside Il Duomo — not just around it
items.sub: Book the rooftop separately. The view of the Alps on a clear day is extraordinary.

items.label: Find Libreria Bocca inside the Galleria
items.sub: Italy's oldest bookshop, open since 1775. Go in even if you don't buy anything.

items.label: Walk the Naviglio Grande at golden hour
items.sub: The canal, the light, the reflections. One of the most beautiful walks in northern Italy.

items.label: Visit Fondazione Prada
items.sub: Former distillery, Rem Koolhaas architecture, Wes Anderson bar. Genuinely extraordinary.

items.label: Stand at a bar for colazione milanese
items.sub: Cappuccino and cornetto, standing. Four minutes. The best way to start any day.

items.label: Explore Isola and see Bosco Verticale
items.sub: The most interesting neighbourhood in the city. The vertical forest towers are unmissable.

items.label: Try cotoletta alla Milanese at a trattoria
items.sub: Bone-in, butter-fried, substantial. Not a schnitzel. Not a side dish.

traps.title: Skip the Traps
traps.intro: Milan is an elegant city, but the Duomo's surroundings hold Italy's record for trap density. Know these four and keep your style intact.

items.name: Corn and bracelets on the Duomo square
items.description: People pressing corn into your hand for pigeon photos or tying a 'gift' string on your wrist will insist on payment afterwards.
items.instead: Hands in pockets, no eye contact, smile and keep walking. Shoot your photo from the square's corner — it looks better anyway.

items.name: Sitting down for coffee in the Galleria
items.description: An espresso at a table in the Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II costs several times the standing price. Most places sell the view, not the coffee.
items.instead: Do it the Milanese way: drink standing at the counter. For historic atmosphere, take the counter side at Camparino.

items.name: 'Free buffet' aperitivo traps
items.description: Some Navigli bars hunt tourists with neon cocktails and a stale buffet; the drink is mediocre, the buffet is a prop.
items.instead: Choose the bar where the crowd speaks Italian; a good aperitivo brings a small but careful plate with your drink.

items.name: Bargaining for 'designer' bags on the street
items.description: The 'Pradas' laid out near Montenapoleone are fake — and buying can be as punishable as selling.
items.instead: For style on a budget, hit the designer outlets or vintage shops; Milan's second-hand is first-class.

callout.label: The golden rule
callout.text: In Milan, quality is quiet: the best places have small signs, plain windows, often a closed door. Avoid anything that shouts.

itinerary.title: Ready-Made Routes
itinerary.intro: If you hate planning, follow these flows. The times are flexible; keep the spirit, break the order.

plans.title: If You Have 1 Day
plans.subtitle: From the Duomo rooftop to a Navigli sunset

steps.title: Duomo + rooftop terraces
steps.description: The cathedral first, then up to the roof: walking among marble spires is Milan's finest moment. Book ahead.

steps.title: Galleria + La Scala
steps.description: Pass through the Galleria (spin on the bull!), emerge at La Scala. The museum is short and sweet if you want a peek inside.

steps.title: Lunch in Brera
steps.description: A trattoria in the painters' quarter; then a quick look into the Pinacoteca di Brera.

steps.title: The Last Supper (with reservation)
steps.description: If you booked months ago, this is your slot. If not, don't grieve: the bone chapel of San Bernardino alle Ossa is an unforgettable plan B.

steps.title: Sforza Castle + Parco Sempione
steps.description: Through the castle courtyard into the park; breathe green alongside the Milanese.

steps.title: Aperitivo on the Navigli
steps.description: Campari or spritz by the canal, the plate that comes with it is your dinner. The peak of the Milanese ritual.

plans.title: If You Have 3 Days
plans.subtitle: Live the city as a guest, not a tourist

steps.title: The icons
steps.description: The 1-day flow above: Duomo, Galleria, Brera, Navigli.

steps.title: Design and fashion Milan
steps.description: Quadrilatero della Moda windows in the morning, Fondazione Prada or Pirelli HangarBicocca at noon, Isola's young bars at night.

steps.title: Hidden Milan and goodbye
steps.description: Villa Invernizzi's flamingos, a whisper into the ear-shaped doorbell of Ca' de l'Oreggia, a Porta Romana spa or vintage afternoon, and a cotoletta farewell.

phrases.title: The 5-Word Survival Kit
phrases.intro: Milan talks fast but never skips its manners; carry these five.

items.meaning: Good morning / good day — mandatory when entering a shop
Please — add it to the end of your order
Cheers! — the official word of aperitivo hour
Let's go! — the key to keeping up with Milan's tempo
